title: India Is Emerging as Asia's Safe Haven as the Global AI Selloff Crushes South Korea and Taiwan
excerpt: With KOSPI plunging below 8,000 and foreigners dumping $137 billion of Asian equities in H1 2026, India's oil-fuelled rally and domestic-demand story are pulling global money in a new direction
body:
As one of the most violent rotations in recent Asian market history plays out, India is emerging on the winning side.

On Thursday, the Nifty 50 rose 0.71% to 24,175.7 and the Sensex climbed 0.75% to 77,502 — a quiet, steady advance that looked unremarkable until you saw what was happening everywhere else. Broader Asian stocks slumped 2.4%. South Korea's tech-heavy KOSPI nosedived roughly 8%, dropping below 8,000 for the first time in weeks. Taiwan, the other AI-driven market darling, extended its own sharp correction.

The trigger was a seismic shift in AI sentiment. Meta Platforms announced plans to monetise excess AI computing capacity rather than continue ramping capital expenditure on new chip infrastructure — a signal that the most capital-intensive phase of the AI buildout may be ending. US semiconductor stocks sold off sharply overnight, and Asia's chip-dependent markets bore the full brunt.

"Tech volatility has prompted a search for alternatives, with India ending June with roughly 3% outperformance and up 7% from the lows in early June," Macquarie said in a note to clients.

The Great Rotation in Numbers

The scale of capital fleeing Asia's AI winners is historic. According to LSEG data, foreign investors pulled a net $137.36 billion from shares across South Korea, Taiwan, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines in the first half of 2026 — the fastest six-month outflow in at least 16 years of records.

South Korea and Taiwan absorbed the bulk of the pain, shedding $70.8 billion and $29.6 billion respectively. The exodus reflects the stunning concentration risk that had built up: the KOSPI nearly doubled in H1, while Taiwan stocks surged 62%, driven almost entirely by three chipmakers — TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix.

"Markets in Asia, there's only two markets and one sector that's outperforming, so at the end of the day, you have to get your balance right," said Joshua Crabb, head of Asia-Pacific equities at Robeco.

> ""Tech volatility has prompted a search for alternatives, with India ending June with roughly 3% outperformance and up 7% from the lows in early June," Macquarie said in a note to clients."

India lost $5.91 billion in June alone — but the context matters. Unlike South Korea and Taiwan, where the outflows represent forced rebalancing from dangerously overweight positions, India's losses are modest relative to its market capitalisation. And the tide is already turning.

Why India Looks Different

Three structural factors are pulling global capital toward Indian equities:

Oil's collapse is India's windfall. Brent crude dropped below $71 per barrel on Thursday after Qatar said Iran and the US had made "positive progress" in indirect talks. Brent is now down 43% from the Iran war peak of $126.41 in April 2026. For India — the world's third-largest oil importer — every dollar off the barrel eases the current account deficit, reduces inflationary pressure, supports the rupee, and gives the RBI room to stay accommodative.

"The drop in oil prices is the single biggest factor for India. It impacts growth, inflation, forex reserves, fiscal deficit — everything," said G. Chokkalingam, founder of Equinomics Research.

The rupee is recovering. The Indian currency has rallied to around ₹94.50 per dollar from an all-time low near ₹97 on May 20, making it one of the best-performing Asian currencies in June. The recovery, supported by RBI measures to encourage dollar inflows and falling crude, has improved dollar returns for foreign investors and removed a key objection to Indian equities.

IT stocks are rebounding on value. The Nifty IT index surged 4.6% on Thursday, leading sectoral gains, after a 6.5% drop over the previous four sessions. Analysts attributed the bounce to value-buying rather than any fundamental shift — but the willingness of investors to step in during a global tech selloff is itself a signal that India's IT sector is being treated as diversified services rather than a pure chip-cycle play.

Global Managers Are Taking Notice

The institutional shift is no longer just talk. "We have gradually reduced our India underweight in the pan-Asia strategies," said Vikas Pershad, a portfolio manager at M&G, which manages roughly $450 billion. The additional capital was freed up by scaling back positions in South Korea and Taiwan.

Christina Woon, head of equity income at Eastspring Investments (managing $270 billion), said she is "incrementally more positive" on India, noting that "valuation opportunities have opened up over the past few months."

Even cautious voices acknowledge the setup is improving. Peeyush Mittal at Matthews Asia noted that improved currency stability and lower oil alone would not be enough — but combined with an earnings recovery forecasted to accelerate from single digits to mid-teens growth, the macro backdrop is constructive.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's comments that inflation expectations have declined in the last four weeks provided an additional tailwind, reducing the risk of further US rate hikes that had weighed on emerging markets.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

For Indian diaspora investors with exposure to Asian markets — whether through ETFs, direct holdings, or retirement portfolios — the message is nuanced:

India's relative outperformance does not make it cheap in absolute terms. Nifty valuations remain above long-term averages, and mid- and small-cap segments, which rose 1.2% and 0.5% respectively on Thursday, have run harder and faster than large-caps.

The real opportunity may lie in the rotation itself. India-focused ETFs like INDA and EPI are natural vehicles for investors who want exposure to the domestic consumption and infrastructure story without the chip-cycle volatility of KOSPI or TAIEX. Sectors insulated from AI disruption — financials (up 0.9% on Thursday, led by Axis Bank and SBI), auto (up 1.2%, with Ashok Leyland and Mahindra surging), and FMCG (up 2.1%, led by Nestlé India and HUL) — offer the clearest relative-value case.

The next catalyst to watch is India's Q1 FY27 earnings season, which begins in mid-July. If earnings growth confirms the mid-teens acceleration analysts expect, the current rotation from AI-heavy markets to India could accelerate further.
